paper_title: The Last Mile to the Real World: Agent-Native Primitives as Reusable Building Blocks for Solving Real-World Tasks

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: How can an agent handle a real-world task end to end? Frontier models with their own harnesses still fall short on real-world benchmarks: on Terminal-Bench 4.0, GPT-5.6 Sol with Codex resolves 37.3% of the tasks and Claude Opus 5 with Claude Code 51.8%. These tasks fail at the step from reaching a resource to applying it, which we call the last mile to the real world. Existing approaches put the resource within reach but leave the competence to apply it with the caller, so each harness rebuilds that competence. We introduce agent-native primitives, reusable units that equip a resource with a resident LLM that applies it in context and communicates with other primitives, and HEELO (Harness Engineering around Evolving Agent-Native Primitives for the Last Mile to Real-WOrld Tasks), a harness engineering framework that builds each task's harness from a library of such primitives. HEELO composes the primitives a task needs into a task-specific graph, verifies the result against evidence from the environment, revises the primitives a failure implicates, and admits new or improved primitives after validation. We instantiate HEELO with eight primitive families, each built for one kind of task, and evaluate them on more than twenty benchmarks. Dev-Primitives raise Terminal-Bench 4.0 resolution from 37.3% under Codex to 55.5% on the same backbone, Harness Primitives composed per task raise Terminal-Bench 2.0 Pass@1 from 60.0% for the seed harness to 72.2%, Tool Primitives raise ToolBench pass rate from 55.8% to 75.1%, and Navigation Primitives raise GAIA-Text-103 accuracy from 45.6% to 58.3%. On the 46 real-world tasks of our heelo.dev platform, Claude Opus 5.5 with Claude Code and GPT-6.1 Sol with Codex complete 9 each on their own and 39 and 35 when connected to HEELO through our MCP server, with 1.9$\times$ and 2.3$\times$ less time and 1.55$\times$ lower cost per completed task.

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: How can an agent handle real-world task end to end? Despite recent progress in LLM agents, frontier models paired with the harnesses built for them still fall short on public benchmarks of real-world tasks: on Terminal-Bench 4.0 at maximum reasoning effort, GPT-5.6 Sol with Codex resolves 37.3% of the tasks and Claude Opus 5 with Claude Code resolves 51.8%. These tasks fail at the step from reaching resource to applying it, which we call the last mile to the real world: tool call must ground its arguments, often in an earlier calls output, each result must reach the steps that consume it, and failure must be traced back to the work it implicates. Existing approaches put the resource within reach but leave the competence to apply it with the caller, so each harness rebuilds that competence. To address this gap, we introduce agent-native primitives, reusable units that equip resource with resident LLM, which applies it in context and communicates with other primitives, and HEELO (Harness Engineering around Evolving AgentNative Primitives for the Last Mile to Real-WOrld Tasks), harness engineering framework that builds each tasks harness from library of such primitives. HEELO composes the primitives task needs into task-specific graph, verifies the result against evidence from the tasks environment and revises the primitives that failure implicates, and admits new or improved primitives into the library after validation. Results proved in our companion studies bound activation by the tasks demand, however large the library, and identify when per-task composition beats the best fixed harness. Each task domain, however, places its own demand on the last mile, so we instantiate HEELO with eight primitive families, each built as the solution to one kind of real-world task, and evaluate them on more than twenty benchmarks. On each comparators backbone, Dev-Primitives raise Terminal-Bench 4.0 resolution from 37.3% under Codex to 55.5%. Over the mini-SWE-agent seed harness, Harness Primitives composed per task raise Pass@1 from 73.0% to 80.5% on 100 SWE-bench Verified tasks and from 60.0% to 72.2% on 45 Terminal-Bench 2.0 tasks, above the 79.0% and 56.7% of Codex. Tool Primitives raise ToolBench pass rate from 55.8% to 75.1%, Code Primitives raise repository delivery from 0.3180 to 0.5134, Agent Primitives raise mean accuracy over eight math, code, and QA benchmarks from 58.8% for single agent to 75.3%, and Navigation Primitives raise GAIA-Text-103 accuracy from 45.6% to 58.3%. In formal theorem proving, Math Primitives place an annotated reference method in the top five for 95.0% of held-out Putnam problems, against 84.2% for the strongest reranker. Further analyses show that the benefit comes from applying each resource inside its primitive and that the task decides which primitives run. Beyond these benchmarks, we built heelo.dev, platform of agent-native primitives for real-world actions. On its 46 real-world tasks, Claude Opus 5.5 with Claude Code and GPT-6.1 Sol with Codex complete 9 each on their own and 39 and 35 when connected to HEELO through our MCP server, with 1.9 and 2.3 less time and 1.55 lower cost per completed task. HEELO provides unified framework for building agents that handle real-world tasks end to end. Keywords: LLM Agents, Agent-Native Primitives, Harness Engineering, Real-World Tasks, LLM Tool Use 1 The Last Mile to the Real World Figure 1: HEELO on public benchmarks and on the real-world tasks of heelo.dev. (a) Each spoke compares HEELO with one baseline: Codex or Claude Code on the same backbone for Dev and Harness Primitives, and otherwise the strongest baseline of the setting. (b) Efficiency per family. (c, d) Claude Opus 5.5 with Claude Code and GPT-6.1 Sol with Codex run the 46 tasks on their own and connected to HEELO through MCP; in (d), time and cost average capabilitys tasks, and marker is filled when every task of its capability is done. The Last Mile to the Real World 1. Introduction Introduction central objective of LLM agents is to complete real-world tasks end to end: to act on the world through tools, code, proofs, documents, and other agents until the tasks own acceptance criteria are met [13]. Recent advances in language models and in the harnesses built around them have improved this ability, as GPT acts through Codex [4] and Claude through Claude Code [5]. Through these harnesses an agent reaches tools and APIs [6, 7], code in large repositories [8, 9], formal proof libraries [10, 11], documents and memories [12, 13], and other agents [14, 15]. Meanwhile, benchmarks increasingly judge agents by whether the real task succeeds: the tool calls fulfil the request, the repositorys tests pass, the answer is correct [6, 1618]. Existing studies have made resources easier to reach and to reuse through tool learning [2, 6, 19, 20], retrieval and memory [12, 2123], skill and code libraries [2426], and multi-agent frameworks, workflow search, and harness generators [15, 2730], providing an important foundation for agents that act in practical environments. Despite this progress, frontier models in the harnesses built for them still fall short on public benchmarks of realworld tasks. On Terminal-Bench 4.0 at maximum reasoning effort, GPT-5.6 Sol with Codex resolves 37.3% of the tasks and Claude Opus 5 with Claude Code resolves 51.8%, and on the four stages of DevOps-Gym the same two pairs average 49.9% and 52.1% success. In the airline domain of 𝜏 2-Bench [31], Claude-4.6-Sonnet succeeds in all four trials on half of the tasks. Tasks as ordinary as booking flight under an airlines policy or filling in form whose later fields depend on earlier answers fail at the step from reaching resource to applying it, which we call the last mile to the real world. Its difficulty shows in three aspects. Application in context: reached resource must be applied to the tasks own objects, as tool call must ground every argument, often in an earlier calls output, and respect the rules of its environment [3234], retrieved code must be adapted to its target and to the components that depend on it [35, 36], proof method applies only where its conditions hold [37, 38], and an answer drawn from documents must stay faithful to its source [39, 40]. Composition: what one step returns or requires must reach the steps that consume it, in form they can use. Evidence-driven revision: failure observed in the tasks environment must be traced back to the work it implicates, so that only this work is redone. Together, these aspects extend the last mile from single call to the whole harness. However, existing approaches keep the resource but leave the competence to apply it with the caller, or fold it into one monolithic agent, so the harness rebuilds this competence for every task: what the caller must read grows with the library, what it learns ends with the task, and its results are hard to check. This raises natural question: how can an agent handle real-world task end to end? To address this gap, we argue that the competence to apply resource should travel with the resource itself, and we introduce agent-native primitives, each reusable resource equipped with resident LLM. The primitive extends reusable software components, temporally extended options, and design by contract [4143] to LLM-based units. The resident LLM is what makes the primitive agent-native: it gives the resource natural-language interface, applies it to each request in context, and communicates requirements to other primitives. Passive artifacts thus become active participants that talk to one another, and the primitives interface lets harness find and invoke it without reading the resource. Primitives alone do not determine which of them task needs, how their results reach one another, which to revise when the task fails, or which new primitives to admit. We therefore introduce HEELO (Harness Engineering around Evolving Agent-Native Primitives for the Last Mile to Real-WOrld Tasks), harness engineering framework that builds each tasks harness, everything the task needs around the model, from an evolving library of primitives through three mechanisms. First, library selection and composition finds candidates through their interfaces or their own relevance assessments and composes the few the task needs into task-specific graph that carries each result and message to its consumer. Second, evidence-based execution and improvement runs the graph in rounds, verifies the result against evidence from the tasks environment, and traces each failure to the primitives it implicates, so that revision redoes their work and keeps the rest. Third, validation and publishing improves the library between tasks, admitting new or improved primitive once evidence such as tests, compiler, or development runs confirms 3 The Last Mile to the Real World Introduction it. Results proved in our companion studies show that need-driven activation stays bounded by the tasks demand, however large the library grows, and identify when per-task composition beats the best fixed harness. However, each task domain places its own demand on the last mile: cooperating agents must combine their work, repository change must reach every component it affects, search must follow what remains unresolved, and harness must fit its task. We therefore instantiate HEELO with eight primitive families, each built as the solution to one kind of real-world task: Tool Primitives for LLM tool use [44], Code Primitives for repository construction [45], Math Primitives for formal theorem proving [46], Knowledge Primitives for knowledge-intensive tasks [47], Agent Primitives for multi-agent systems [48], Dev-Primitives for software engineering [49], Navigation Primitives for large information spaces [50], and Harness Primitives for agent harnesses [51]. Each family realizes the definition above and the mechanisms its task needs, so the eight companion studies become instances of one framework. For these families, we build 25,519 Tool Primitives, 16,464 of them wrapping live APIs; 1,424 Code Primitives, each validated against the tests it carries; and 82 Math Primitives whose Lean artifacts compile. We also introduce benchmark of 522 repository-reconstruction tasks drawn from real Python projects in seven domains. Extensive experiments on more than twenty benchmarks demonstrate that, on the same backbones, Dev-Primitives outperform Codex by 18.2 points on Terminal-Bench 4.0, and Harness Primitives composed per task exceed the mini-SWE-agent seed harness by 7.5 and 12.2 points and Codex by 1.5 and 15.5 points on 100 SWE-bench Verified and 45 Terminal-Bench 2.0 tasks, for composition cost of 2.7% to 4.3% of one actor attempt. Code Primitives surpass Claude Code on its backbone by 56.2% in repository delivery and keep 95.1% of their delivery at 24.0% lower cost with GPT-OSS-20B adaptation and diagnosis. Tool Primitives on Qwen3-8B lead every reference model on 𝜏 2-Bench at up to 7.7 lower cost than GPT-5.4 and complete 2.63.8 as many of 50 curated real-world tasks as GPT-5.4, Claude-4.6-Sonnet, and Gemini-3.1-Pro calling the same tools. Agent Primitives on Qwen3-8B exceed the strongest prior multi-agent system by 7.5 points with 34 fewer tokens than text-based one, Navigation Primitives lead the strongest GAIA-Text-103 baseline by 12.7 points, and with GPT-5.6 Luna, Knowledge Primitives gain 14.3 points over Hybrid RAG on average and Math Primitives lead the strongest reranker by 10.8 points in Putnam hit@5. Further analysis across families reveals that the gain lies inside the primitive and that the task decides which primitives run: Tool Primitives more than double the ToolBench pass rate of budget-matched selfrefinement over raw schemas, and active Navigation Primitives grow 1.23 while distractors grow the information space 16 around the same evidence. Beyond these research benchmarks, we build heelo.dev, platform through which agents such as Claude Code, Codex, or Cursor invoke real-world actions as agent-native primitives, from publishing pages and sending outreach to reading invoices and scraping sources. Its 46 real-world tasks cover the 26 capabilities of four end-to-end loops, with the pass criteria of each task fixed before its first run. On their own, Claude Opus 5.5 with Claude Code and GPT-6.1 Sol with Codex, both at medium reasoning effort, complete 9 of the tasks each, with mean task scores of 28% and 25%. Connected to HEELO through our MCP server, Claude Code completes 39 and Codex 35, with scores of 90% and 83%. Per completed task, Claude Code with HEELO needs 3.4 minutes and $0.80 instead of 6.3 minutes and $1.24 on its own, and Codex with HEELO 3.5 minutes and $0.42 instead of 8.0 minutes and $0.65. HEELO thus provides unified framework for handling real-world tasks end to end. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: We introduce agent-native primitives under one definition that pairs reusable resource, from tools, code components, and proof methods to source models, multi-agent patterns, and repository files, with resident LLM that applies it in context and messages other primitives. We further build libraries of 25,519 Tool Primitives, 1,424 validated Code Primitives, and 82 Math Primitives with Lean-checked scaffolds. We propose HEELO, one harness engineering framework that unifies the eight families: each tasks harness is graph composed from an evolving library and revised where the tasks evidence implicates it, and the library grows between tasks with validated primitives, so that new kind of task can join as new primitive family. 4 The Last Mile to the Real World Related work Experiments on more than twenty benchmarks across eight kinds of real-world tasks show that every family improves on its reference baseline: primitives lead Codex by 18.2 points on Terminal-Bench 4.0 and Claude Code by 56.2% in repository delivery, and cost up to 7.7 less than GPT-5.4 on 𝜏 2-Bench. Cross-family analyses locate the gain inside the primitive and show that the task decides which primitives run. We build heelo.dev, platform that exposes real-world actions, from flights and calendars to email and browser automation, as agent-native primitives to agents such as Claude Code, Codex, or Cursor. On its 46 real-world tasks in four end-to-end loops, Claude Code and Codex complete 9 tasks each on their own and 39 and 35 when connected to HEELO through MCP, with 1.9 and 2.3 less time and 1.55 lower cost per completed task. 2. Related Work Tool Learning and Interfaces. LLM agents learn to call tools from self-annotated data [2], large collections of real-world APIs [6, 7], and synthesized singleand multi-turn function-calling data [19, 52, 53], while compact models make function calling robust on device [54]. Benchmarks span structured calls and tool-augmented dialogue [20, 55], large-scale, compositional, and nested call sequences [32, 56, 57], and stateful, conversational environments [31, 33, 34, 58], while AgentDojo evaluates tool-using agents under adversarial prompt injection [59]. OpenAPI, the Model Context Protocol, Agent2Agent, and Agent Skills make services, tools, agents, and packaged instructions discoverable [6063]. Across these settings, the caller binds each call itself: it writes schema-compliant arguments and grounds each value in the intended object, often an earlier calls output. Tool Primitives move schema binding into the tool, so that the caller states its need in natural language and resident LLM conditioned on the tools schema produces the typed call. Code Reuse and Repositories. Software reuse made interfaces, dependencies, and adaptation cost central to building systems from components [41, 64]. Learned systems discover libraries and abstractions [6567], make tools for later tasks [26, 68, 69], retrieve code and documentation during generation [35, 70, 71], and distill reusable procedures from agent experience [72, 73]. Repository-level agents inspect, edit, and execute code [3, 8, 9], follow explicit localization and repair stages [74, 75], or divide work among task graphs, roles, and coordinated developers [7678]. Evaluation ranges from cross-file and repository-level generation [36, 79] and issue repair [16] to long-horizon evolution [80], repository generation and whole-repository migration [81, 82], and terminal and DevOps workflows [17, 83]. In these systems, the reused artifact stays fixed while central agent decides how to use it, and the units of reasoning and their connections are designed in advance or kept inside one trajectory [84, 85]. Code Primitives make adaptation an operation of the reused component, and Dev-Primitives route requirements along the repositorys own dependencies. Retrieval, Memory, and Knowledge. Retrieval-augmented generation brings external content into model computation [12, 86, 87], adaptive methods decide when and what to retrieve [40, 8891], and long-context models use evidence unevenly across positions [39]. Reading-comprehension benchmarks ask model to combine what it reads, through discrete reasoning over paragraphs in DROP [92] and multi-hop reasoning in HotpotQA [93]. Beyond flat passages, structured representations organize source into summary trees [21], graphs [9496], associative or global memories [9799], and task-conditioned structures [100]. Agent memories keep interactions [13, 101104], feedback [22], insights [23], skills [24], and workflows or procedures [25, 105] across tasks. In large information spaces, retrieval chooses its next query from the remaining gaps [106108], and multi-agent readers divide long inputs [109, 110] or retrieval, filtering, and planning [111113] among workers. What persists in these methods is the corpus, structure built from it, or experience from interaction, and when readers divide long inputs among workers, coordination grows with how the space is partitioned, regardless of what the query requires. By contrast, Knowledge Primitives keep revisable model of one authoritative source and commit only the revisions that the source supports, and Navigation Primitives let unresolved information needs decide which primitives run. Formal Theorem Proving. Lean and Mathlib give provers checked proof language and large reusable library [10, 11]. LLM provers generate whole proofs or repair them from verifier feedback [114116], and agentic 5 The Last Mile to the Real World Related work loops alternate generation with Lean-guided repair [117, 118]. Retrieval-augmented proving, premise selection, and declaration search supply formal facts [119121], and lemma libraries grow across problems [122]. Such retrieval ranks fact, lemma, or prior proof by relevance, and LLM rerankers that reason about fit report score or an ordering [123126], leaving the prover to decide how to use candidate. Proof planning describes methods by their conditions and effects [37, 38], and adaptation-guided retrieval prefers cases that adapt to new problem [127, 128]. Math Primitives bring this view to LLM provers: Method Contract carries methods required conditions, intended action, and residual obligations, and each contract proposes its use on the goal before ranking. Multi-Agent Systems and Communication. Multi-agent frameworks organize LLMs by assigning predefined roles [15, 129], programming conversations among customizable agents [14], recruiting collaborators iteratively [130], or letting agents debate [131, 132]. Other methods design the team automatically: DyLAN selects agents by estimated value [133], GPTSwarm optimizes collaboration graphs [27], and MAS-GPT generates configuration from the query [134]. Recent methods communicate below text by sharing learned latent space [135], projecting or propagating keyvalue caches [136, 137], or aggregating experts through cross-attention [138]. For cache messages, rotary embeddings make keys position part of its meaning [139]. These systems take the agent or the team as the unit of design, and the latent methods mainly improve how information passes between agents. Agent Primitives make recurring multi-agent computation pattern the reusable unit and implement its computation structure through latent KV cache communication, with all agents on one LLM so that their inputs and outputs stay aligned. Agent Harnesses and Workflows. The harness around model decides how observations, memory, retries, and checks shape its actions: ReAct interleaves reasoning with actions [1], Reflexion and Self-Refine feed verbal feedback into later attempts [22, 140], and DSPy compiles declarative pipelines of model calls [141]. Codex and Claude Code, the platform harnesses built for GPT and Claude, supply the tools and execution loop around these frontier models [4, 5]. Design methods search over agent programs and workflows [28, 29] or edit and evaluate candidate harnesses to select one for all tasks [142, 143]. Others adapt the harness at test time, specializing it for each case from retrieved execution experience [144] or rewriting harness code and generating task-specific modules [30, 145]. These methods fix one harness across tasks, specialize it through instructions that the actor must follow, or write new control code at test time, which must then be implemented, debugged, and validated. Harness Primitives validate each control operation when it enters the library, so that tasks harness is selected and compiled from implemented parts before the actor runs. Key Differences. Across these lines of work, the units (a function, code component, lemma, passage or memory, role or team, harness) keep resource but leave the competence to apply it with the caller or fix it in an agent design. An agent-native primitive keeps that competence with the resource by equipping it with resident LLM: the primitive owns the resource, exposes an interface through which harness finds and invokes it, applies the resource to natural-language request in context, and communicates with other primitives; where domain offers an exact procedure, program replaces the resident LLM. HEELO selects and composes primitives per task, revises only what the evidence of failure implicates, and publishes improved primitives through validation path separate from task execution. Eight primitive families instantiate this design on eight kinds of real-world tasks. Overall, primitives let the harness of real-world task be engineered around reusable, validated units. 3. Methodology Figure 2 gives an overview of HEELO. We first state the problem of building harness for real-world task and define the agent-native primitive from which the harness is built. We then describe the three mechanisms that build and run each tasks harness and improve the library between tasks, the eight primitive families that instantiate the method on eight kinds of real-world tasks, and three properties of the selection that decides which primitives run, each proved in companion study. The Last Mile to the Real World Methodology Figure 2: Overview of HEELO. Top: the agent-native primitive library, one box per family with the resource its primitives own. Middle: real-world task enters as task request with its context, constraints, and acceptance criteria; library selection and composition finds candidates through their interfaces, lets each assess its own relevance, and composes task-specific graph whose activated primitives exchange messages, and three illustrative compositions are drawn on the right. Bottom: evidence-based execution runs and verifies the plan in the tasks environment, improvement traces failure to the implicated primitives and revises only that work within round budget, and validation and publishing adds validated primitive to the library on separate path. The bottom strip shows what an agent-native primitive holds: resource, resident LLM that serves as its natural-language interface, an interface through which harness finds and invokes it, and an output of results and messages to other primitives. 3.1. Problem Formulation real-world task 𝑞 arrives with context 𝑐𝑞: its inputs, its environment, its constraints, and the acceptance criteria by which it is judged (the task request of Figure 2). An agent acts on the task through harness 𝐻, the control program between the model and the environment. The harness decides which operations run, with which inputs, in which order, and when the run stops. Running 𝐻 on 𝑞 produces trajectory 𝜏 . The tasks own acceptance procedure, such as its tests, its proof checker, or its answer key, scores the trajectory as 𝑅𝑞(𝜏 ) [0, 1], and we write 𝑅(𝑞, 𝐻) = E𝜏 [𝑅𝑞(𝜏 ) 𝐻]. fixed harness, such as one general-purpose coding agent, uses the same 𝐻 for every task. Following our companion study on Harness Primitives [51], we build the harness of each task from library ℒ of reusable units: 𝐻𝑞 = 𝐹 (𝑞, 𝑐𝑞; ℒ) ℋ(𝑐𝑞), 𝐻 * 𝑞 arg max 𝐻ℋ(𝑐𝑞) 𝑅(𝑞, 𝐻), (1) 7 The Last Mile to the Real World Methodology where ℋ(𝑐𝑞) is the set of harnesses compatible with 𝑐𝑞. The construction procedure 𝐹 approximates 𝐻 * 𝑞 from the units of ℒ, within budget on model calls or revision rounds. While 𝐹 builds and runs 𝐻𝑞, it keeps context 𝒞𝑡 for round 𝑡, which starts as 𝒞0 = 𝑐𝑞 and accumulates results and feedback. The last mile lies inside Eq. (1) at two levels. Each unit of ℒ must be applied to the tasks own objects, and 𝐹 must decide which units the task needs and how their results combine. HEELO answers the first level with agent-native primitives and the second with the mechanisms that realize 𝐹 . 3.2. Agent-Native Primitives unit of the library helps task only once it is applied in context. tool call must ground its arguments, retrieved component must be adapted to its target, proof method must be instantiated on the goal, and an answer must stay faithful to its source. caller that applies every unit itself rebuilds this competence for each task and must hold the details of every unit it uses in one context [44, 49]. An agent-native primitive keeps this competence with the unit by equipping the unit with resident LLM that applies it. Definition 3.1 (Agent-native primitive). An agent-native primitive 𝑃𝑖 equips reusable resource 𝑎𝑖 with resident LLM ℳ and exposes an interface 𝑑𝑖 through which harness finds and invokes it. Invoked with natural-language request 𝑥𝑖 in context 𝑐𝑖, the resident LLM, conditioned on the resource, applies 𝑎𝑖 and returns result 𝑟𝑖 together with the messages 𝑚𝑖 = {𝑚𝑖𝑗}𝑗 that the primitive addresses to other primitives 𝑃𝑗: the requirements that 𝑟𝑖 places on them, or task-relevant information they need, with 𝑚𝑖 = when none is needed: (𝑟𝑖, 𝑚𝑖) = 𝑃𝑖(𝑥𝑖; 𝑐𝑖) = ℳ([ 𝑎𝑖; 𝑐𝑖; 𝑥𝑖 ]), (2) where [] denotes the input context of the resident LLM. The resident LLM is what makes the primitive agent-native. It reads the resource and serves as its natural-language interface, sparing the caller from holding the resources details in its own context. The primitives messages carry requirements and task-relevant information to other primitives. Resources that were passive artifacts thus become active participants that reason locally and communicate with one another. The resource 𝑎𝑖 can be anything the task relies on, from tools schema and function to repository component, proof method, or source model, and the interface 𝑑𝑖 is what harness reads in its place, such as tools schema descriptor or the selection side of Method Contract. One base model can serve as the resident LLM of every primitive of library, conditioned on different resource each time, so primitive is defined by the resource it owns. Where domain offers an exact procedure, as for the control operations of Harness Primitives, implemented code applies the resource and receives its request as parameters. resource that downstream prover or solver consumes, such as the execution side of Method Contract or source model, is applied by that model. Relevance Assessment. Similarity between request and an interface does not show that primitive applies. primitive can therefore assess its own relevance before it is selected [45, 46]: (𝑠𝑖, 𝑢𝑖) = ℳassess(𝑃𝑖, 𝑥, 𝒞𝑡), (3) where 𝑠𝑖 judges whether 𝑃𝑖 applies to request 𝑥 derived from the task, and 𝑢𝑖 proposes how 𝑃𝑖 would be used. Run over the whole library at once, this assessment removes the dependence on pool that similarity retrieval chooses first (Proposition 3.3). Carried Validation. resource may carry its own means of validation, such as tests or schema. The primitive applies them before it returns and reports structured failure when they fail. Carried validation shows that the primitives own step succeeded. Whether the result serves the task is for the harness to decide. Library. Primitives form library ℒ = {𝑃𝑖}𝑁 𝑖=1. library is either built ahead of the tasks that draw on it and reused across them, or induced from tasks own data, such as repository or an information space [49, 50]. library built ahead of its tasks does not change while task runs. An induced library follows the tasks data and can change as the task edits that data. 8 The Last Mile to the Real World Methodology 3.3. Harness Engineering around Agent-Native Primitives Primitives determine how each resource is applied. They do not determine which primitives task needs, how their results reach one another, or what to change when the task still fails. Two mechanisms realize the construction procedure 𝐹 of Eq. (1): library selection and composition builds the harness, and evidencebased execution and improvement runs and revises it. third mechanism, validation and publishing, improves the library between tasks (Figure 2). Library Selection and Composition. primitive sees only the request it is handed, so it cannot decide alone whether the task needs it. library also usually holds more primitives than one task uses. COMPOSE therefore finds candidates through their interfaces, either by retrieval or by reading every interface at once. Eight Primitive Families The method above is shared across tasks, but each task domain places its own demand on the last mile: cooperating agents must exchange their intermediate state, repository change must reach the components that depend on it, search must follow the needs that remain unresolved, and harness must fit its task. We therefore instantiate HEELO with eight primitive families, each built as the solution to one kind of real-world task, and the primitives of family own the resource that its task applies, from the tools of LLM tool use and the components of repository construction to the proof methods of formal theorem proving and the control operations of agent harnesses. The families differ in how they specialize the method, as summarized below in each familys own terms and notation, so that symbol such as 𝐹 , 𝑀 , or 𝑅 keeps the meaning of its own study within its paragraph. We provide the full framework of each family, with its overview figure, in Appendix B. Tool Primitives. Tool Primitive [44] wraps one ToolFace tool: its resource 𝑎𝑖 is the schemafunction pair (𝑠𝑖, 𝑓𝑖), and its interface 𝑑𝑖 is the schema descriptor. The shared model conditioned on the schema, 𝒫𝑖(𝑥; 𝑐) = ℳ([𝑠𝑖; 𝑐; 𝑥]), maps the request 𝑥 to the arguments of 𝑠𝑖 and invokes 𝑓𝑖, returning the result with summary or structured failure. HEART is the harness engineering framework around Tool Primitives, and its COMPOSE has three parts: request decomposition asks the user for missing details and writes an invocation plan, semantic search over schema descriptors retrieves candidate tools for each step, and value resolution grounds each steps values in the query and earlier results; each steps result is the context 𝑐 of the next. Tool Primitives for LLM Tool Use LLM tool use places the smallest demand on the last mile: each tool does what the task needs, and what remains is to call it correctly. In function calling, the model writes schema-compliant arguments for each call [2, 7, 20] and maps one tools output into the next tools input schema, step that nested and multi-turn calls make brittle, while large catalogue in context degrades performance [39]. Tool Primitives reverse this burden: instead of requiring models to speak the language of APIs, they make tools speak the language of models [44]. Each Tool Primitive 15 The Last Mile to the Real World Experiments resolves the schema of its own tool, and HEART, harness engineering framework, decomposes each query into an invocation plan, grounds each steps arguments, and validates every returned result (Section 3.4). Code Primitives for Repository Construction Repository construction asks an agent to deliver complete project whose modules, interfaces, configuration, tests, and dependencies work together [81]. When the project reuses code, the last mile lies in making that code fit its target. component reused from another repository becomes part of the delivered source, so its signatures, data representations, and dependencies must be reconciled with the target. Retrieval-augmented code generation finds related code [35, 70, 71] but leaves this reconciliation to the caller. Code Primitives assign it to the component itself: each Code Primitive adapts the implementation it owns to the target and checks the result against the tests it carries, while LEGO retrieves, coordinates, and verifies these primitives during construction [45]. Math Primitives for Formal Theorem Proving In formal theorem proving with Lean 4 and Mathlib [10, 11], the kernel checks each completed proof, and LLM provers generate and revise proofs against this check [114, 115, 117], aided by premise selection, Mathlib search, and lemma libraries [119122]. Here the last mile is deciding whether method applies: which part of the goal it targets, what action it takes there, and which conditions that action requires. For 𝑛 𝑖 𝑎𝑖)2 over the reals, similarity retrieval proposes AMGM, which needs 𝑎𝑖 0, condition the goal does not give, while Cauchy Schwarz applies. Math Primitives let the library speak instead: each holds proof method as Method Contract, and under self-advertised method selection every contract proposes how it would be used on the goal before the contracts are ranked [46]. 𝑖 ( 𝑖 𝑎2 Setup. We place each problem by the rank of its highest-ranked annotated method under self-advertisement with 20 The Last Mile to the Real World Experiments GPT-5.6 Luna and by that methods rank under BM25 and each embedding retriever (Figure 17 in Appendix C). This is the candidate-pool ceiling of Proposition 3.3(ii) at work: reranker reorders the pool that similarity retrieved, so no reranking backbone recovers method that the pool omits. Self-advertisement judges all 82 contracts, and each method it brings into the shortlist arrives with target, an action, and required conditions that can be checked against the goal. Method Contract stays fixed once built, whereas Knowledge Primitives source model changes as the agent studies its source. 4.5. Knowledge Primitives for Knowledge-Intensive Tasks When many tasks draw on one persistent, authoritative source, such as document collection, code repository, or API documentation, the last mile is understanding that source: how its knowledge is structured, interpreted, and applied, beyond the passages that one task retrieves. Retrieval brings such passages into each task [12, 86], structured indexes organize the sources content [21, 94, 98], and agent memories keep experience from earlier tasks [22, 23, 25], yet repeated use of source is still treated as repeated access. Knowledge Primitives turn this repeated use into source learning: the resource of Knowledge Primitive is persistent source model that holds reusable source-specific competence, while the source itself remains the authority for factual content. SourceLearn [47] develops this source model in two ways. Before future tasks are known, Self-Directed Source Learning studies what the source model does not yet explain well, and Task-Guided Source Learning uses guidance tasks to expose local gaps and recurring needs in how the source is represented. We provide the full framework of SourceLearn in Appendix B.4, together with its overview figure, the benchmark and baseline settings, and the comparison at matched context budget. Setup. We evaluate SourceLearn on question answering over document collections, stories, and code repositories with MultiDoc2Dial [146], NarrativeQA [147], and SWE-QA [148]; tool use with APIBench [7]; and interactive tasks with AppWorld [149]. Each document collection, story, repository, or API library is one source. Guidance and test tasks are disjoint, with three fixed 30%/70% splits and AppWorlds official training and test-normal splits. GPT-5.6 Luna judges QA answers against the references, and APIBench and AppWorld use their official evaluators. The baselines are task-local retrieval with Hybrid RAG, persistent source representations with RAPTOR [21] and HippoRAG 2 [98], and experience-based memory with AWM [25], which learns workflows from the same guidance tasks. Each configuration uses single backbone, GPT-5.6 Luna [170], GPT-OSS-120B [172], or DeepSeek-V4.1Flash [171], for the LLM operations of all methods, which share the embedding model, the answer or agent prompt, and, on AppWorld, the ReAct-style code agent [1]. SourceLearn adds the activated source model to the Hybrid RAG evidence 𝑅(𝐷, 𝑞), which AWM also receives, so the comparison with Hybrid RAG isolates the contribution of the source model. Main Results. Across the 15 settings of Table 9, SourceLearn is the best method in 13 and the second best in one more. It improves on Hybrid RAG in 14 settings, and its average gain over the five benchmarks is 14.3 pp with GPT-5.6 Luna, 4.9 pp with GPT-OSS-120B, and 13.4 pp with DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. The gains span document, code, and API sources and exceed 10 pp on four of the five benchmarks with GPT-5.6 Luna and with DeepSeekV4.1-Flash; with GPT-5.6 Luna, MultiDoc2Dial rises from 64.9% to 77.6% and APIBench from 47.8% to 70.4%. The two settings in which it is not the best both use GPT-OSS-120B: HippoRAG 2 leads on SWE-QA (56.7% against 53.4%), and on AppWorld SourceLearn falls below Hybrid RAG (27.4% against 30.4%). The baselines help unevenly. RAPTORs summary tree falls below Hybrid RAG on SWE-QA under all three backbones, where HippoRAG 2 is the strongest baseline, and AWM, the strongest baseline on APIBench, moves question-answering accuracy by at most 3.9 pp. Learning the source transfers across benchmarks more evenly than structuring its content or retaining task experience. Analysis. Both learning mechanisms contribute and complement each other. We remove each in turn with GPT5.6 Luna on two sources of each QA benchmark, with the splits and task-time source access of the main results (Figure 9). The full model 𝑀𝑇 is the most accurate on all three benchmarks, omitting Self-Directed or TaskGuided Source Learning lowers accuracy, and the initial model 𝑀0 is the lowest. Within Task-Guided Source Learning, removing failure-guided local refinement or cross-task representation learning lowers accuracy on all three benchmarks, and removing both, which recovers the self-directed model 𝑀𝑆, lowers it further. The two pathways thus carry different information from the same guidance tasks: concrete failures repair local gaps, while recurring representation lessons change how the whole model represents the source. Learning also does more than compress the source (Figure 19). From 𝑀0 to 𝑀𝑇 , the model shifts from isolated look-up content toward rules and procedures, and the share of units with an explicit applicability condition rises from roughly 30% to 6582% on the four MultiDoc2Dial sources. The share of the claims required by test questions that the model represents rises from 23.2% to 40.0%, and questions with all of their required claims represented are answered correctly 86.6% of the time, against 67.5% when none are. The Tool, Code, Math, and Knowledge Primitives each own resource that single model applies; Agent Primitives own recurring multi-agent computation pattern, whose agents run on one LLM and exchange KV caches. 4.6. Agent Primitives for Multi-Agent Systems Where several agents share one problem, the last mile lies in how they combine their work. Multi-agent systems (MAS) let LLM agents critique, vote, and plan together, but they are usually designed task by task, with handcrafted roles and interaction prompts, so their complexity grows with the task, and no reusable abstraction amortizes it. Their agents also communicate in natural language, which degrades over long, multi-stage interactions. In two stress tests with Qwen3-8B, an instruction injected at the midpoint of long context is followed in 15.6% of cases through text and in 73.3% through KV caches, and after ten unrelated sentences are injected into solved GSM8K traces, 47% of the problems stay solved through text and 93% through KV caches. Agent Primitives [48] address both problems with three reusable latent building blocks, Review, Voting and Selection, and Planning and Execution, 22 The Last Mile to the Real World Experiments whose internal agents communicate through KV caches and which an LLM Organizer composes into primitivebased MAS for each query. Navigation Primitives for Large Information Spaces In large information space, the requirements of query change as evidence arrives: new evidence can resolve or refine requirement, reveal another, and redirect the search [187]. At the last mile, coordination must therefore follow what remains unresolved, whereas partition-driven multi-agent systems such as LongAgent [109] and Chain of Agents (CoA) [110] assign one member to each chunk of the input, so their coordination grows with the space. Navigation Primitives are workers that each search one territory of the space, and ANTMAN [50] coordinates them through revisable Need Graph that tracks querys unresolved information needs and decides which primitives take part in the search (Section 3.4). Across these experiments, unresolved needs decide which Navigation Primitives run, under control program that is the same for all queries; Harness Primitives compose that program itself for each task. 4.9. Harness Primitives for Agent Harnesses For fixed task-solving model, the actor, an agents success depends on its harness: the control program that constructs the actors requests, executes its actions through the available tools, returns observations, and decides when to terminate [51, 143]. The last mile then reaches the harness itself, which must fit the task. Hand-designed harnesses such as SWE-agent [8] and Codex [4], and the harnesses that optimizers such as MetaHarness find, apply one design to all tasks, yet mechanism that improves one task can impose overhead or context distraction on another. Generating harness code for each task avoids this mismatch but adds generation and debugging cost, with execution risks that compound as more mechanisms are generated. Harness Primitives make task-specific harnesses possible without generating or repairing mechanism code at test time. They are control operations implemented and validated during development, each with an application scope and composition contract, and STITCH [51] selects the primitives that suit each task and compiles them into its harness before the actor starts. Setup. We evaluate on 100 randomly sampled tasks of SWE-bench Verified [16], which asks for repairs of real repository issues, and on 45 randomly sampled tasks of Terminal-Bench 2.0 [17], which covers tasks in terminal environment; results are broken down by repository (Django, SymPy, and the others) and by difficulty. Both samples are disjoint from the 100 SWE-bench and 44 Terminal-Bench development tasks on which the primitives were developed. Each task gets two attempts, and we report Pass@1, the fraction of successful attempts; Pass@2, the fraction of tasks solved in at least one attempt [183]; and Pass2, the fraction solved in both. GPT-5.6 Luna at medium reasoning effort [170] serves as both the actor and the composer, and GPT-5.6 Sol is the development model. The baselines are the mini-SWE-agent 2.4.6 seed harness [8], SWE-agent, Codex, and the harness optimizers MemoHarness [144] and MetaHarness [143], which start from the same seed. STITCH exceeds the best fixed primitive by 4.5 pp on SWE-bench Verified and by 5.5 pp on Terminal-Bench 2.0, whereas the random composer, at 73.3% and 63.5%, stays within the range of the fixed primitives. The breakdowns show why fixed choice falls short: the same primitive can help on some tasks and hurt on others. Contract-case Explorer raises Pass@1 above the seed on the other repositories, 77.9% against 69.1%, but lowers it on Django, 69.2% against 75.0%, and on SymPy no fixed primitive reaches the seeds 75.0%, which STITCH matches. On Terminal-Bench 2.0, State Guard leads the fixed arms on medium tasks but lowers easy-task Pass@1 from 100.0% to 83.3%, while Execution Supervisor leads them on hard tasks; STITCH reaches 81.0% on medium and 46.2% on hard tasks and keeps 100.0% on easy ones. This is the task-mechanism mismatch behind Proposition 3.2: fixed harness either pays primitives penalty outside its application scope or forgoes its gain inside it. Composition also scales with the library. Growing the test-time library along one order of addition, from the seed harness (size 0) to eight entries on SWE-bench Verified and six on Terminal-Bench 2.0, raises Pass@1 from 73.0% to 80.5% and from 60.0% to 72.2% (Figure 15). Transfer and Cost. The primitives and the composer carry over to actors not used in development. With implementations and contracts unchanged and the scopes adjusted on development tasks, STITCH averages 84.0% Pass@1 on SWE-bench Verified over GPT-5.6 Terra, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and Claude-4.5-Haiku, against 75.2% for the seed, 78.5% for Codex, and 79.5% for the best fixed primitive  (Table 34)  ; with the GPT-5.6 Terra actor, Codex leads at 88.0% against 86.5%. Each fixed primitive also stays above the seed on this average, so the primitives encode control mechanisms that generalize across actors. Composition is cheap and reliable. It costs 4.3% of one actor attempt on SWE-bench Verified and 2.7% on Terminal-Bench 2.0; lower bound for writing the complete harness at test time, which counts an oracle coders output tokens alone, is about 543 and 638 the cost of composition. Each selected primitive activated and executed without runtime errors (Figure 16): the selected primitives take effect during the actors execution, free of the reliability risk of generated harness code. We provide the full framework of STITCH, its overview figure, and the per-actor, library-size, and composition-cost results in Appendix B.8. 31 The Last Mile to the Real World 5. Analysis Analysis We further analyze the gains of Section 4 by setting the controls of the eight companion studies side by side. The analysis asks four questions: where the benefit of primitive comes from, what the channels between agents and primitives carry, what decides which primitives run and what is revised after failure, and what task costs and where strong model pays off. Each question draws on more than one family, so its answer concerns the method that the eight families share. 5.1. Where the Benefit Comes From With the backbone and the reused resources fixed, the controls below vary how primitive applies the resource it owns (Definition 3.1), what it carries, and how much of the library its assessment reaches. Application versus Access. At matched backbone, calls, and tokens, the gain comes from the primitive, which extra inference does not replace. HEARTs budget-matched control reallocates the calls of the Tool Primitives to value resolution, which self-refines its arguments over raw schemas; with Qwen3-8B, it reaches 34.2% ToolBench pass rate, against 75.1% with Tool Primitives  (Table 26)  . Nor does access to the same components suffice. When LEGO shows the caller the retrieved components with their contracts and tests as read-only context, delivery reaches 0.3544, close to the 0.3469 of diagnosis without any library and below the 0.5134 of Code Primitives  (Table 6)  . Primitive Fields. Most of the margin over generic editing lies in the fields of 𝑃𝑖  (Table 28)  . generic editor over the same retrieved components scores 0.4093, and adding the carried tests 𝑉𝑖, the interface contract and provenance 𝐼𝑖, 𝑋𝑖, and the dependency closure 𝐷𝑖 raises it to 0.5039, within 0.0095 of primitive adaptation (𝑝 = 0.49) [45]. Withholding 𝑉𝑖 from an otherwise complete primitive lowers delivery to 0.4796. Source-Model Content. source model adds more than context. When each retrieval counterpart receives SourceLearns per-question context budget, filled from further down its own ranking, SourceLearn leads on three of the four sources tested with GPT-5.6 Luna  (Table 29)  . On the QA benchmarks with Luna, its gain over Hybrid RAG is 12.1 pp on regions that no guidance task touched and 14.9 pp on touched regions  (Table 45)  . Reach of Assessment. Assessment over the whole library reaches what reranking of retrieved pool misses. By Proposition 3.3(ii), the hit@𝑘 of any reranker of similarity pool is capped by whether the pool holds an annotated contract (Eq. (10)). Across three selector backbones, the best reranker of top-10 pool plateaus between 0.842 and 0.858 Putnam hit@5, while self-advertisement over all 82 contracts (Eq. (3)) reaches up to 0.975  (Table 7)  . Tool Primitives are found by similarity retrieval and so face the same ceiling, which is high here: retrieval over the 25,519 schema descriptors of ToolFace places 95.8% of ToolBench and 97.2% of NESTFUL gold tools in its top ten  (Table 35)  . Validation and Grounding Audits. HEARTs result validation agrees with human labels on 200 sampled ToolBench and NESTFUL decisions at 0.97 precision and 0.96 recall, with an 8% false-pass rate  (Table 36)  , so the failures it reports can drive revision (Section 5.3) [44]. SourceLearns grounding audit finds 13.3% and 3.3% of the sampled units of the final StudentAid and pytest source models unsupported by the source elements they cite, while the fully supported share of the HuggingFace model rises from 65.0% to 84.2%  (Table 43)  . The source model therefore complements the source, which stays authoritative and directly accessible [47]. Together, these controls place the benefit in what the primitive owns and in applying it where it lives. What primitive returns must then reach the agents and primitives that use it. 5.2. Communication Within and Between Primitives What crosses between agents and primitives carries part of the result (Section 3.3). Two families each disrupt one channel while keeping backbones, primitives, and components fixed. The Last Mile to the Real World Analysis KV Cache Communication. Agent Primitives run all agents on one LLM, so that one agents cache is readable by another. When receiver reads senders cache after its own system-level cache, the senders keys are reindexed to their new positions to preserve RoPE semantics [139]. Without this re-indexing, the composed MAS on R1/Llama-70B falls from 85.3% to 31.1% on HumanEval+, and on Qwen3-8B it loses 13.3 pp on AIME25  (Table 30)  . Each primitive used alone on R1/Llama-70B also loses 26.7 to 59.7 pp, so the loss already arises in the KV cache communication inside each primitive, before any composition [48]. Messages Between Dev-Primitives. Dev-Primitives directed message 𝑚𝑖 carries the task-relevant information or requirements that it communicates to other components (Section 3.4). With GPT-5.6 Sol, removing these messages while keeping each Dev-Primitives local reasoning and edits lowers the SWE Refactor Bench composite from 31.0 to 23.5 and Terminal-Bench 4.0 resolution from 51.8% to 46.1%, larger drops than on SWE-bench Verified (97.0 to 94.2), consistent with messages coordinating changes that span files  (Table 15)  . On Terminal-Bench 4.0, one editor given the same plan and components resolves 38.8%, and 45.5% at matched compute, against 51.8% for HERMES  (Table 32)  , so component-local reasoning with direct communication leads at equal compute. In both families, cache read at the wrong positions or requirement that never reaches its component costs accuracy, although each agent and Dev-Primitive performs its own step as before. 5.3. Activation and Revision With the primitives and their channels fixed, COMPOSE decides which primitives run (Eq. (4)), and revision decides what changes after failure (Eq. (6); Figure 2, middle and bottom). For ANTMAN and STITCH, the interventions below examine the behaviour that Propositions 3.1 and 3.2 predict. Space and Demand. ANTMAN satisfies the premises of Proposition 3.1: each step routes one unresolved need to at most one territory-backed worker (Eq. (48)), and each need is routed at most 𝜌 times. Participation accordingly follows demand and changes little with the size of the space: it grows 1.23 when distractors grow the space 16 around the same evidence, against 15.29 and 15.33 for the members of LongAgent [109] and CoA [110]  (Table 17)  , and it reaches 8.0 workers when the required evidence grows to 16 units in fixed space  (Table 18)  . Excess Activation. Activating more than the task needs costs accuracy as well as calls. Keeping all Dev-Primitives identified in HERMESs initial analysis active throughout raises primitive calls from 9.6 to 28.7 per SWE-bench Verified task and lowers the score on each of the four benchmarks by 1.2 to 3.0 points (Tables 15 and 52). Task-Conditioned Choice. Per-task composition beats the best fixed choice, and random composition falls to the level of the fixed choices. STITCHs fixed primitives raise Pass@1 on some repositories and difficulty levels and lower it on others (Section 4.9), the heterogeneity that Proposition 3.2 needs. With the GPT-5.6 Luna actor, per-task composition reaches 80.5% Pass@1 on SWE-bench Verified, against 76.0% for the best primitive applied to all tasks and 73.3% for random composer  (Table 20)  , and Terminal-Bench 2.0 keeps this order  (Table 21)  . The Organizer of Agent Primitives composes per query and reaches 73.3% on Qwen3-8B AIME25  (Table 10)  . Random structures from its Knowledge Pool reach 66.7%, the level of the best single primitives, and the Organizer without its pool reaches 63.3%. With Claude-4 as the Organizer, composition also reaches 73.3% (Tables 46 and 47). For Agent Primitives, the benefit thus comes mainly from problem-aware structure selection and not from particular Organizer model [48]. For Harness Primitives, it comes from choosing complementary primitives for each task [51]. Library Size. Growing STITCHs test-time library of accepted primitives along one order of addition raises Pass@1 from 73.0% for the seed harness (size 0) to 80.5% at size 8 on SWE-bench Verified and from 60.0% to 72.2% at size 6 on Terminal-Bench 2.0 (Figure 15). Drivers of Revision. Removing the mechanism that turns evidence from the run into revision (Eq. (6)) lowers the result in each family that ablates it. Result validation is HEARTs sole judgment of whether steps result answers the query; without it, ToolBench pass rate falls from 75.1% to 47.6%, the same value as with no revision rounds (Tables 4 and 37). Without the diagnosis feedback that names the components that revision reactivates 33 The Last Mile to the Real World Analysis (Eq. (45)), HERMESs Terminal-Bench 4.0 resolution falls from 51.8% to 41.2%, the largest drop among its four mechanism removals  (Table 15)  . Without task-local recovery of stalled needs, ANTMANs 512K F1 falls from 84.03 to 60.12  (Table 19)  . Across these interventions, the task decides what runs and what is revised: its unresolved needs bound participation, its features select the composition, and the evidence of its failures and stalled needs decides what changes. 5.4. Cost and Model Allocation What runs and what is revised also sets what task costs, which each study records in its own unit. Per-Task Cost. At matched cost, reuse delivers more: execution feedback with eight attempts reaches 0.3437 delivery at $2.07 per task, against 0.5134 at $2.08 for Code Primitives, which lead at each attempt limit (Tables 27 and 40). Composing Harness Primitives costs 4.3% of one actor attempt on SWE-bench Verified and 2.7% on Terminal-Bench 2.0, while the output-token lower bound for an oracle that writes the complete harness is about 543 and 638 the cost of composition (Figure 16). As the space grows 16, ANTMANs calls grow 1.21 and its cost 6.90, against cost growth of 14.22 for LongAgent and 16.11 for CoA  (Table 17)  . Strong-Model Placement. For Dev-Primitives, whose LLM can differ from the activation and diagnosis models, strong model pays off most in diagnosis  (Table 50)  . With GPT-5.6 Sol in activation and diagnosis, Qwen3-8B DevPrimitives resolve 50.6% of Terminal-Bench 4.0 tasks, against 27.6% with Qwen3-8B in all three roles. stronger diagnosis model alone raises resolution to between 44.5% and 47.9%, and stronger activation model alone to at most 38.2%. Sol activation with Qwen3-8B Dev-Primitives and GPT-5.5 diagnosis reaches 49.7% at $2.13k, against 51.8% at $3.40k with Sol in all three roles, 2.1-pp loss for 37.4% lower expenditure  (Table 51)  . Smaller Models Inside Primitives. With GPT-OSS-20B as the resident LLM of all Code Primitives and as the diagnosis model, LEGO keeps 95.1% of its delivery (0.4880) at 24.0% lower recorded-call cost  (Table 27)  . ANTMAN-H, which runs all components except the GPT-4.1 orchestrator on Qwen3-8B, reaches 57.3% against 58.3% on GAIA-Text-103 and 25.0% against 41.7% on its hardest level  (Table 16)  . With GPT-5.4 in decomposition, value resolution, and result validation and Qwen3-8B in the Tool Primitives, HEART reaches 𝜏 2-Bench Pass1 of 0.84, 0.75, and 0.67 on retail, airline, and telecom, close to the 0.86, 0.78, and 0.68 of GPT-5.4 in all roles (Appendix B.1) [44]. In these three families, as in Dev-Primitives, smaller model takes the work inside the primitives while stronger model coordinates. Summary. Across the four questions, the analyses locate the benefit in applying each resource inside its primitive, in what the primitive carries, in channels that keep their meaning, and in activation and revision controlled by the task. At matched budgets the primitives deliver more, and smaller models inside them keep most of the result at lower cost while stronger model coordinates. The end-to-end outcome of real-world task thus depends both on the competence that each primitive keeps with its resource and on the mechanisms that HEELO builds around the primitives (Section 3.3), which each family realizes as its task needs. 6. The heelo.dev Platform for Real-World Tasks On the research benchmarks of Section 4, as in the cross-family protocol of Appendix E, the environment is frozen and the grader is fixed in advance. Real-world tasks also run against live services, accounts, and people. To test HEELO under these conditions, we built heelo.dev (https://heelo.dev), platform that exposes real-world actions as agent-native primitives (Figure 3), and we compared agents with and without HEELO on 46 such tasks. 6.1. Platform Overview heelo.dev is tool execution backend for AI agents. It exposes third-party actions, such as flights, calendars, email, social posting, company research, and browser automation, as tools behind one invocation endpoint, and each tool 34 The Last Mile to the Real World The heelo.dev platform Figure 3: The heelo.dev platform. Agents such as Claude Code, Codex, or Cursor reach real-world tools through HEELO, which orchestrates agent-native primitives for each task: it plans the task, routes each need to primitive, executes the primitives, and verifies the result, revising the plan when check fails. Four loops test the platform end to end: distribution creates and publishes content across channels, acquisition finds potential customers and sends personalized outreach, the personal assistant takes over everyday tasks across apps and tools, and validation discovers real problems and validates market demand. follows the agent-native design of Section 3.2. tool accepts the fields of its input schema or natural-language request and encapsulates its own execution strategy, from LLM calls to browser automation and third-party APIs, and it keeps its state in session. When request lacks detail, the tool returns clarification question with the sessions identifier, and the caller continues the session until the tool returns result or an error. Callers reach the tools in four ways: direct invocation; natural-language router that selects tool from the descriptions and examples of all registered tools; ReAct loop that chains tools step by step, each result informing the next action; and an MCP server through which external agents, such as Claude Code, connect to HEELO. Tool calls are recorded in shared log. 6.2. Four Real-World Loops The real-world tasks of the platform are organized as four loops, each with one end-to-end task  (Table 22)  . Each loop adds three tool families to the platform, such as mail.read, doc.extract, and doc.render for the assistant, and draws on tools that the platform already has, such as calendars, Notion, and the posting tools of single platforms. Distribution publishes campaigns content to several channels, each under its own platform rules, and hosts the pages that capture visitors. Acquisition finds people and companies with matching need and sends them multi-step outreach from an authenticated domain. The assistant turns an invoice email into checked fields, approved writes, and receipt, and validation mines the problems that people report and tests the demand for one of them. The loops also feed one another: distribution attributes each click from acquisitions outreach to the contact who clicked and stops that contacts sequence once the contact is captured, and validation reaches real people through acquisition. loops task is therefore solved only when the tools compose within loop and across loops, each tools result reaching the tool that consumes it. Codex scores zero on the funnel math with and without HEELO: its answers compute the rate but leave out the caveat of small sample. Of the two end-to-end tasks, Claude Code with HEELO passes all 12 runs of the shorter one and Codex with HEELO 7. In the six-stage end-to-end validation, Claude Code with HEELO passes stages two to four, up to launch that finds 110 people at 77 companies, and Codex with HEELO stops before the assessment, because its fresh scans return no assessable problem. 38 The Last Mile to the Real World Conclusion Time and Cost. In most tasks, connected run costs more than run on its own, because it reads more tokens, from the tool menu to the structured results of the primitives: the median assistant run of Claude Code with HEELO reads 160,701 tokens and takes 23.4 seconds, against 19,456 tokens and 9.4 seconds on its own. Because the connected agents complete most of their tasks, they need less time and lower cost per completed task: Claude Code with HEELO needs 3.4 minutes and $0.80, against 6.3 minutes and $1.24 on its own, and Codex with HEELO 3.5 minutes and $0.42, against 8.0 minutes and $0.65, which is 1.9 and 2.3 less time and 1.55 lower cost. Per completed task, Codex with HEELO is the cheapest of the four arms. Repeated work also costs less with HEELO: when task revisits JavaScript page whose extraction recipe heelo.dev stored on the first visit, the second visit costs less than half the first in every run of both connected agents, against one of three runs of Codex on its own. Across the four loops, the gap between an agent on its own and the same agent connected to HEELO opens where task must act on an account or service: an agent on its own can find page, draft message, or write script, but published page, sent sequence, or an invoice read from mailbox takes primitive that holds the account, applies its resource in the tasks context, and verifies the outcome before it reports success. 7. Conclusion How can an agent handle real-world task end to end? Our answer is to engineer each tasks harness around agent-native primitives, which address the last mile to the real world by keeping the competence to apply resource with the resource itself. An agent-native primitive equips resource with resident LLM that applies it to natural-language request in context and sends other primitives the requirements that its result places on them; where the domain offers an exact procedure, program takes the place of the resident LLM. HEELO builds each tasks harness from library of such primitives through three mechanisms. Library selection and composition retrieves and assesses candidates and composes the few that the task needs into task-specific graph. Evidence-based execution and improvement runs the graph, verifies its result against evidence from the tasks environment, and after failure revises only the primitives that the evidence implicates, within budget of revision rounds. Validation and publishing admits new or improved primitives into the library only after validation, on path separate from any task. Each of the eight primitive families comes from the solution we built for one kind of real-world task, realizes the mechanisms that its task needs, and improves on the reference baseline of its companion study. On the tasks where frontier harnesses fall short, Dev-Primitives lead Codex by 18.2 points on Terminal-Bench 4.0 with GPT-5.6 Sol at maximum effort, and composing Harness Primitives per task raises Terminal-Bench 2.0 Pass@1 from 60.0% for the seed harness to 72.2%, above the 56.7% of Codex. The analyses show that binding inside Tool Primitive beats budget-matched self-refinement over raw schemas and that the fields Code Primitive carries account for most of its margin over generic editing. What crosses between agents and primitives must keep its meaning: exchanged KV caches need positional re-encoding, and requirements must reach the components they concern. The task, in turn, decides which primitives run, as active Navigation Primitives grow 1.23 while distractors grow the information space 16 around the same evidence. The families share one method, so new kind of task can join HEELO as new primitive family that realizes the same definition and mechanisms. Beyond the research benchmarks, heelo.dev exposes real-world actions to agents as agent-native primitives. On its 46 real-world tasks, Claude Code and Codex complete 9 tasks each on their own and 39 and 35 when connected to HEELO through MCP, with 1.9 and 2.3 less time and 1.55 lower cost per completed task. Overall, primitives let the competence developed for one task outlast that task: once validated and published, the primitive that carries this competence becomes building block that later tasks compose. 39 The Last Mile to the Real World

Tool Primitives: Natural-Language Invocation and Harness Engineering Tool Primitives give each tool natural-language interface [44], and HEART, Harness Engineering framework via Agent-native, Reusable Tool Primitives, makes these primitives practical at repository scale. Harness Engineering. HEART supplies what the abstraction leaves undetermined with three mechanisms. Request decomposition is needed because primitive answers the request it is handed and cannot ask what the user wants. Intent analysis identifies the target task and its objective, the relevant tool categories, and the users explicit constraints or preferences. Information sufficiency checking then decides whether the context 𝒞𝑡 of query, acquired information, and execution history supports fully specified plan: 𝛿𝑡 = DECOMPOSE(𝑞, 𝒞𝑡) {sufficient, insufficient}. (13) While 𝛿𝑡 = insufficient, decomposition returns to the user targeted clarification request 𝑐𝑡 for the missing information, and the reply enters the context. It then writes the invocation plan Π = (𝜋1, . . . , 𝜋𝐾), whose steps give tool category, tool hint, the steps objective, and the steps it depends on. Value resolution is needed because steps values come from the user query and from earlier results, which the primitive does not see. It resolves the values of step 𝜋𝑘 from 𝒞𝑡 into natural-language invocation request 𝑥𝑘 that names the target Tool Primitive and embeds the values inline, together with execution hyperparameters: 𝛽𝑘 = RESOLVE(𝜋𝑘, 𝒞𝑡) = (𝑥𝑘, H-Params𝑘 ). (14) Values may come from the query, earlier clarifications, or the result of any upstream step, referenced as $step_j. <field>. Code Primitives: Adaptation with Carried Tests Code Primitives are reusable software components that adapt their implementations, interfaces, and dependencies to target repositories [45]. Tool Primitives and Agent Primitives expose tools and reusable behaviours through interfaces that support invocation; Code Primitive instead provides an interface for adaptation, because it becomes part of the delivered repository. LEGO, Large-scale repository Engineering via aGent-native reusable cOde primitives, builds repositories with Code Primitives drawn from CodeFace, library mined once from real repositories. Adaptation is performed by the component that owns the implementation, while constraints that cross components are resolved at the repository level. SourceLearn [47] is the framework that develops this model 65 The Last Mile to the Real World Framework details Figure 8: Overview of SourceLearn. Task-Guided Source Learning uses guidance-task failures and recurring representation needs to further refine the model into 𝑀𝑇 . At inference time, Source-Model Activation combines relevant source-model context with directly retrieved evidence for downstream tasks [47]. through repeated study and use of the source, and we describe it in its own notation: 𝑀 is source model, 𝐹 the task solver, 𝐵 token budget, 𝑅(𝐷, 𝑞) the source context of task 𝑞 and 𝑅 alone source region, and Π0 and Π1 are instructions on how to represent source. Initial construction builds provisional source model 𝑀0 from the source 𝐷, Self-Directed and Task-Guided Source Learning refine it into 𝑀𝑆 and then 𝑀𝑇 through grounded source reconstruction, and at test time the solver receives the activated 𝑀𝑇 beside the retrieved evidence (Figure 8). Problem. persistent authoritative source 𝐷 grounds recurring tasks (𝑞, 𝑦) 𝒫𝐷, where 𝑦 is the desired outcome of 𝑞. Knowledge access, source learning, and the use of the learned understanding are ˆ𝑦 = 𝐹 (𝑞, 𝑅(𝐷, 𝑞)), 𝑀𝑡 = Learn(𝐷, 𝐻𝑡), ˆ𝑦 = 𝐹 (𝑞, 𝑅(𝐷, 𝑞), 𝑀𝑡 ), (26) where 𝑅 may be retrieval, long-context access, or structured source representation, and 𝐻𝑡 is the accumulated study and task experience. Repeated access alone can leave reusable knowledge fragmented or in need of reconstruction for each task. Source learning therefore faces two questions: what source knowledge to learn before future tasks are known, and how task feedback can improve source-specific competence beyond the task that produced it, since retaining an observed answer or correction risks learning the task rather than the source. Self-Directed Source Learning addresses the first question and Task-Guided Source Learning the second: 𝑀0 = Construct(𝐷), 𝑀𝑆 = SelfLearn(𝐷, 𝑀0), 𝑀𝑇 = TaskLearn(𝐷, 𝑀𝑆; 𝒢), (27) where 𝒢 = {(𝑞𝑡, 𝑦𝑡)}𝑇 𝑡=1 holds guidance tasks grounded in the same source, with reference outcomes 𝑦𝑡. Source Model. 𝑀 is organized around source entities 𝑒, each with reusable representation 𝑚𝑒 of its properties, mechanisms, governing conditions, procedures, exceptions, distinctions, and relations to other entities, and higherlevel structure organizes dependencies across entities. Each unit makes one reusable semantic commitment and 66 The Last Mile to the Real World Framework details cites the source elements it rests on; facts that reader can look up stay in 𝐷. Construct reads the source entity by entity within coherent regions, such as code modules or document sections, under generic modeling instruction Π0 that favors major entities, relations, procedures, and governing conditions over redundant low-level content. The resulting 𝑀0 is deliberately provisional. Grounded Source Reconstruction. All later updates follow one principle: learning signals determine what should be reconsidered, while persistent knowledge is reconstructed from the authoritative source. For an affected source region 𝑅 and learning signal 𝜉, 𝑂𝑅 = Inspect(𝐷𝑅, 𝑀𝑅; 𝜉), 𝑀 = GroundApply (𝑀, Reconstruct(𝑀𝑅, 𝑂𝑅); 𝐷𝑅 ), (28) where the temporary observations 𝑂𝑅, gathered by rereading the regions source content against the current model, are never copied into 𝑀 . Each proposed unit passes through the grounding gate, which judges statement supported when its cited excerpts entail it and negative claim supported when an excerpt states the denial; any other unit counts as unsupported. Agent Primitives: Reusable Latent Building Blocks Agent Primitives [48] address two limitations of existing multi-agent systems (MAS): they lack reusable, taskagnostic abstraction for organizing multi-agent computation, so their complexity scales with task complexity, and they communicate in natural language, which degrades in long contexts and under accumulated noise. Drawing on neural network design, where complex models are built from reusable blocks such as residual blocks and attention heads [191], the study decomposes existing MAS architectures into few recurring, minimal computation patterns, such as iterative review, multi-agent consensus, and planexecute decomposition, and instantiates three representative primitives that communicate via keyvalue (KV) cache. Communication Bottleneck. Two stress tests with Qwen3-8B [169] motivate KV cache as the medium. In longcontext task injection, an auxiliary instruction is injected at the beginning, midpoint, or end of the long contexts of 351 En.QA examples from InfiniteBench. Without injection, natural-language communication reaches 51.6% accuracy and KV cache communication 61.3%. At the midpoint, injection compliance falls to 15.6% for natural language, against 73.3% for KV cache, while accuracy stays stable across positions, so the degradation stems from communication failure. In communication noise, 100 correctly solved GSM8K [153] traces, truncated to 6,000 tokens, are continued by another Qwen3-8B within 5,000 tokens while 0 to 25 sentences of unrelated reasoning are injected. With one and three noise sentences, natural language solves 91% and 73% of the problems and KV cache all of them; with 10 and 25, 47% and 40% against 93% and 77%. Primitive Design. Internal coordination runs exclusively through latent KV cache exchange, so primitives behavior is independent of text-level message passing, and each primitive can serve as drop-in replacement for single agent. The role system prompts fix role boundaries independently of task-specific content and encode no explicit problem-solving strategy. Review, an iterative self-critique operator, connects Solver 𝐴 and Critic 𝐵 through latent feedback channel: 𝐵 consumes the KV cache of 𝐴 to generate corrective feedback, and the modified latent representation returns to 𝐴 for refinement until stopping condition derived from the intermediate latent states holds, which gives adaptive depth of refinement. The Critic provides evaluative signals and neither revises the solution nor answers. In Voting and Selection, consensus operator, parallel Solvers produce latent candidates independently, and Selector votes and selects over these candidates directly in latent space, computing an aggregated latent state that produces the output; it judges correctness, consistency, and overall solution quality without introducing reasoning beyond the candidates. In Planning and Execution, latent decomposition operator, Planner 𝑃 produces latent plan that decomposes the task into intermediate steps or subgoals without solving it, and an Executor 𝐸 follows the plan without modifying it to generate the output. Primitive-Based MAS. primitive-based MAS is composition graph of primitives, which an LLM Organizer, GPT-5.2 by default, builds per query. The Organizers prompt supplies the query, the three primitives, and the Knowledge Pool, and instructs it to analyze the task requirements and complexity, to select primitives, and to determine their execution order and composition structure. The Organizer reasons at the level of primitives, designs no task-specific roles or natural-language protocols, and does not solve the task. Its primitive composition plan specifies (i) the primitives to instantiate and (ii) their execution structure in code, at 200400 output tokens per query. The lightweight Knowledge Pool holds 45 previously observed queries paired with effective MAS structures from frameworks including Multi-Agent Debate [131], DyLAN [133], Self-Refine [140], AFlow [29], and MAS-GPT [134]. The Organizer retrieves entries by the input query as structural guidance and abstracts them into primitive compositions, replacing task-specific agents with Agent Primitives. The system then executes the plan, coordinating within and across primitives through KV cache, and externally behaves like standard MAS. Implementation. Navigation Primitives: Need-Conditioned Coordination Navigation Primitives are scope-specialized workers, each searching one territory of an information space, and ANTMAN [50], an adaptive coordination framework, decides which of them search for query. ANTMAN answers query 𝑞 from an information space ℐ whose available information can grow large while the information that 𝑞 requires stays comparatively small. Newly encountered information can change the searchers understanding of the problem and redirect the search [187], so ANTMAN makes evolving unresolved information needs the runtime control state for coordination, which lets worker activation and search decisions adapt as those needs change. Evaluation Settings. Multi-document QA scores 30 questions from each of HotpotQA [93], 2WikiMultiHopQA [157], and MuSiQue [158] for nine methods, 810 predictions in all, with one frozen answer-extraction and evaluation pipeline, and its baselines also run on GPT-4.1. In the space intervention, each per-length entry averages 30 evaluations, ten questions with evidence at early, middle, and late positions. The demand study uses ten matched 512K base contexts, each with 16 planted evidence records over fixed pool of eight territories; documents, distractors, evidence locations, territory assignment, and WorkerCards stay fixed across demand levels, while the query and its gold answer change with the level. Runs are capped at ten coordination rounds, answers are scored by exact match, and Complete Evidence counts unit as recovered when its content is extracted, rather than when its document is accessed. The ablations use the 512K condition, 40-question SWE-QA-Pro subset sampled with seed 42, and fixed 40-question GAIA subset. E. Evaluation Protocol for Cross-Family Composition This appendix specifies an evaluation of HEELO as one system that composes primitives of several families. Its experiments measure what the three results of Section 3.5 predict, namely activation against realized demand (Proposition 3.1), the gap between task-conditioned and fixed composition (Proposition 3.2), and the reach of retrieval stage (Proposition 3.3), together with the reliability of the verification that each family brings. Stress Conditions and Statistical Analysis Concurrency experiments should run concurrent tasks over one shared library, which no task changes (Section 3.3), with conflicting and disjoint edits. In LEGO and HERMES, primitive edits only the component it owns and passes cross-component requirements, within the same round, to the primitives that must satisfy them; conflicting edits test this ownership when primitives of different families touch the same artifact. Drift experiments should revise API schemas, source documentation, runtime dependencies, and model compatibility while measuring invalidation and revalidation.
